planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; this is one of the oldest and toughest named selections of the species itself, prized for reliability in brutal winters.

directions: Rounded trusses of rosy-lilac to lavender flowers open in late spring over a dense dome of large, leathery evergreen leaves, and this nineteenth-century French selection of the straight Appalachian species is still sold specifically for its unusually dependable cold hardiness. It tends to flower a little later than many hybrids, which can help dodge a late frost that would otherwise ruin the buds. Keep roots cool and evenly moist with a thick mulch layer, avoid soggy or alkaline sites, and prune only right after bloom to preserve next year's flower buds. Because it is a selection of the wild species rather than a complex hybrid, it also makes a genetically useful planting near other catawbiense-derived cultivars for comparison in native plant collections.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; this dwarf selection of the species stays dense and low, making it useful for foundation plantings or hedging where full-size catawbiense would outgrow the space.

directions: A naturally compact, slow-growing form of the wild Appalachian species, this selection covers itself in rounded trusses of purplish-lavender flowers each late spring without ever reaching the towering size of a straight-species catawbiense. Its tighter habit and smaller leaves make it a good choice for mass plantings, low hedges, or smaller gardens that still want the bomb-proof hardiness the species is known for. Mulch well to keep the shallow roots cool and moist, site it out of winter sun and wind to prevent leaf scorch, and deadhead spent trusses to encourage stronger bloom the following year. It combines easily with other ironclad hybrids bred from the same parent species.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; this old catawbiense-derived ironclad hybrid is grown for dependable, vivid red bloom in climates too cold for most red rhododendrons.

directions: Rounded trusses of bright red flowers with a darker, faintly brown-flecked blotch cover this nineteenth-century hybrid in late spring above dense, dark evergreen foliage on a sturdy, rounded shrub. Bred using the native Appalachian species as its hardy backbone, it remains one of the standard choices for gardeners in cold regions who want true red flower color without sacrificing winter reliability. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, water during dry spells since the root system stays shallow, and shelter from harsh winter sun and wind to prevent leaf burn. Deadhead and prune immediately after flowering, since next year's buds form soon afterward.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; one of the oldest and most cold-tolerant white-flowered catawbiense hybrids, valued for reliability over fussier modern whites.

directions: Buds that open blush-lilac fade to a soft near-white as the large, dense trusses mature in late spring, set against bold, leathery evergreen foliage on a vigorous, broad-spreading shrub. Raised in the nineteenth century from the native Appalachian species, it has outlasted many later white hybrids thanks to tougher cold tolerance and a forgiving nature in average garden soil. Mulch generously to protect the shallow roots, keep it out of drying winter wind, and water through dry summer stretches rather than letting it wilt. Prune right after the flowers fade if it needs shaping, since the following year's buds set quickly afterward.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; a Victorian-era catawbiense hybrid still grown today for strong rosy-crimson color and dependable cold hardiness.

directions: Dense, rounded trusses of rosy-crimson flowers open in late spring over large, dark evergreen leaves on a broad, well-furnished shrub that has stayed in commerce since the 1860s for good reason. Descended from the native Appalachian species, it tolerates harsher winters and poorer soil than many showier modern hybrids while still delivering a strong, saturated flower color. Mulch to keep the shallow roots cool and consistently moist, avoid wet or heavy clay sites, and water during extended dry spells. Prune immediately after bloom if size control is needed, since flower buds for the following season form soon after petals drop.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; a long-lived Victorian-era catawbiense hybrid grown for rose-pink flowers and proven toughness in cold regions.

directions: Full, rounded trusses of clear rose-pink flowers marked with a faint brownish-red blotch appear in late spring on a dense, well-branched shrub clothed in large, dark evergreen leaves. Bred from the cold-hardy Appalachian species in the nineteenth century, it has remained a dependable garden plant precisely because it shrugs off harsh winters and indifferent soil better than many later, fussier hybrids. Keep the shallow root zone mulched and evenly moist, give it afternoon shade where summers run hot, and prune only right after flowering to protect next year's buds. Established plants are long-lived and need little more than an annual mulch refresh.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; one of the oldest catawbiense hybrids still sold, notable for frilled, ruffled petal edges unusual among hardy rhododendrons.

directions: Lilac-pink flowers with distinctly frilled, wavy petal margins and a light greenish-gold blotch gather into full trusses in late spring, a trait that sets this 1850s hybrid apart from the smoother-edged blooms typical of most catawbiense-derived cultivars. The dense, rounded shrub carries handsome dark evergreen foliage year-round and has remained available for well over a century thanks to its combination of distinctive flowers and reliable cold hardiness. Mulch to protect the shallow roots, provide partial shade and shelter from winter wind, and water during dry periods rather than letting the shallow root zone dry out. Prune right after bloom if needed, since buds for the next season set quickly.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; a mid-1800s catawbiense-derived hybrid prized for deep crimson-purple flowers and exceptional cold hardiness.

directions: Compact, rounded trusses of rich crimson-purple flowers open in late spring against a dense mound of dark, leathery evergreen leaves on a shrub that has been grown in gardens since the mid-nineteenth century. Its deep, saturated flower color stands out among the more pastel catawbiense hybrids, while its cold hardiness keeps it reliable in regions where showier red and purple rhododendrons often fail. Mulch well to keep the shallow roots cool and moist, site it away from drying winter sun and wind, and water through dry spells in its first few seasons. Deadhead and prune immediately after flowering to keep the shrub tidy and encourage strong bloom the following year.
